content: When delamanid is administered as part of the multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) regimen, the first dose is typically taken alongside other medications in the regimen. However, the second dose of delamanid is often taken separately, necessitating careful treatment supervision to ensure adherence. Injectable agents, if absolutely required, are generally administered intramuscularly once daily, and the dose should not be divided, except for imipenem-cilastatin and meropenem, which are given intravenously in divided doses. Oral agents are usually taken daily throughout the week. Bedaquiline is administered daily for the first two weeks, followed by three times weekly for the subsequent 22 weeks. If a patient misses all medications scheduled for a given day, treatment should resume the following day, with an additional day added to the end of the regimen. However, during the first two weeks of treatment, missed doses should not be made up, and the usual dosing schedule should continue without extending the two-week period. From the third week onward, if a 200 mg dose of bedaquiline is missed, the patient should take the missed dose as soon as possible and then resume the three-times-weekly schedule. For missed delamanid doses, the patient should take the dose as soon as possible unless it is close to the time of the next scheduled dose, in which case the missed dose should be skipped. Double dosing to compensate for missed doses is not recommended. For MDR/RR-TB patients on longer regimens, a total treatment duration of 18–20 months is generally suggested, with adjustments based on the patient’s response to therapy. For those who achieve culture conversion, a treatment duration of 15–17 months post-conversion is recommended. In regimens containing amikacin or streptomycin, an intensive phase of 6–7 months is suggested, though this may also be modified based on therapeutic response. All-oral longer regimens do not include an intensive phase. The total treatment duration may need to exceed 18–20 months in cases with additional drug resistance, depending on clinical response. Milk and dairy products can reduce the absorption of certain fluoroquinolones. For children, the World Health Organization (WHO) recommends the use of bedaquiline in those aged six years and older and delamanid in those aged three years and older. Delamanid exposure in children aged 3–5 years has been achieved using a dispersible 25 mg tablet, which is also available under compassionate use. Splitting, crushing, or dissolving the 50 mg delamanid tablet may alter its bioavailability. Injectable-containing regimens are particularly undesirable in children, and shortening the treatment duration to less than 18 months may be considered for children without extensive disease. For severe forms of extrapulmonary TB, including TB meningitis, WHO recommendations for longer MDR-TB regimens also apply, with adjustments based on the disease location. Treatment of MDR/RR-TB meningitis should be guided by drug susceptibility testing (DST) and the ability of TB medications to cross the blood-brain barrier. High-dose isoniazid and pyrazinamide can achieve therapeutic levels in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and may be useful if the strains are susceptible. However, PAS and ethambutol do not penetrate the central nervous system (CNS) well and should not be relied upon for MDR-TB meningitis. Amikacin and streptomycin only penetrate the CNS in the presence of meningeal inflammation. Data on the CNS penetration of clofazimine, bedaquiline, or delamanid are limited. Meropenem is preferred over imipenem for TB meningitis in children due to a lower risk of seizures. In pregnancy, data on the safety of bedaquiline and delamanid are limited. Observational studies suggest that fetal exposure to bedaquiline in utero may be associated with low birth weight but no other significant differences in infant or maternal outcomes. Longer regimens during pregnancy should be individualized to include components with established safety profiles. Outcomes of treatment and pregnancy, as well as postpartum surveillance for congenital anomalies, should be documented to inform future recommendations. For monitoring treatment response in MDR/RR-TB patients on longer regimens, monthly sputum culture is strongly recommended in addition to sputum smear microscopy. Monthly culture has higher sensitivity in predicting treatment outcomes compared to smear microscopy alone, reducing false negatives and improving the detection of true positives. Combined use of smear microscopy and culture helps identify patients whose bacteriology remains positive or reverts to positive after initial conversion, enabling timely adjustments to treatment and infection control measures. Regular microscopy and culture remain critical for early detection of treatment failure, and culture monitoring at six and 12 months post-treatment completion is advised to ensure sustained cure. In children, monitoring treatment response through smear and culture can be challenging due to difficulties in obtaining bacteriological confirmation. For children with confirmed diagnoses, efforts should be made to demonstrate bacteriological conversion. Clinical improvement, including symptom resolution and weight gain, can serve as indicators of treatment success. Regular clinical follow-up, including weight and height monitoring, is essential, and drug dosages should be adjusted as needed with weight gain. The bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL) regimen, lasting 6–9 months, has been studied for MDR-TB with additional fluoroquinolone resistance. The Nix-TB study in South Africa demonstrated the safety, efficacy, and tolerability of this regimen, though it was associated with a high rate of adverse events, including potential reproductive toxicity. The BPaL regimen is recommended for use under operational research conditions conforming to WHO standards, including ethical approval, patient-centered care, informed consent, and active drug safety monitoring. Pretomanid, a novel medication, is not recommended outside the context of the BPaL regimen due to limited experience with its use in other combinations.
